traveler: Saint Erasmus of Formia (Erasmo, Sant'Ermu, St Elmo)
title: The Windlass and the Fire: Erasmus of Formia, from a Contested See to a Light on the Masthead
years: birth unrecorded, traditionally c. 250 - c. 303; cult continuous to the present
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Antioch, the birth no register holds
stops.date_confidence: unrecorded. No source gives a birth year, and the two traditions do not agree on a birthplace: en.wikipedia 'Erasmus of Formia' and CatholicSaints.info offer Mount Lebanon, the Antioch strand and it.wikipedia offer Antioch. 250 is arithmetic run backwards from a traditional death of 303, entered as a placeholder to keep the file sortable, not as a datum.
stops.campa: No register anywhere records the birth. Tradition puts it on Mount Lebanon or in Antioch, the great Syrian city where the roads out of Persia meet the sea and where the followers of Christ were first called Christians. The name given the child is Erasmus, the beloved. Everything after this comes from a Passio written some two and a half centuries later by an author nobody has identified, in a Latin that no longer knows which of two cities it means. The year is arithmetic run backwards from a death, not a datum.
suggested_refs: The site of Roman Antioch beneath modern Antakya, Turkey

stops.name: Formia, the see the Latin West gives him
stops.date_confidence: traditional. No source from his own century names him at all. The earliest hard anchor in the entire dossier is a letter of Gregory the Great, roughly three hundred years later, saying where the body is kept.
stops.campa: Erasmus is bishop of Formia in Campania, a Roman harbour town on the Appian Way between Rome and Naples, in the years before Diocletian's edict. Jacobus de Voragine will credit him with the whole of Italian Campania. This is the see the Latin West keeps, and the see the relics belong to. Its town will be burned out from under him six hundred years later. Nothing written in his own century names him. The first solid thing in the file is a pope, three centuries on, reporting a location.
suggested_refs: The Roman harbour of Formiae on the Appian Way, extinguished as a see after 842
sources: Jacobus de Voragine, Golden Legend, via en.wikipedia

stops.name: Antioch, the see the Italian tradition gives him
stops.date_confidence: contradiction, flagged and not resolved. it.wikipedia calls him outright vescovo di Antiochia. en.wikipedia makes Formia his see and treats an Erasmus of Antioch as a separate Syrian bishop whom the Acts of Saint Elmo have folded into him. Both pins stand in this file, six hundred miles apart, on the same date. Neither is preferred.
stops.campa: The Italian article calls him outright vescovo di Antiochia. The English article makes Formia his see and treats an Erasmus of Antioch as a distinct Syrian bishop whom the Acts of Saint Elmo have folded into him. The two national traditions do not agree and no source consulted resolves them. Either a Campanian bishop has been given a Syrian youth, or a Syrian bishop has been given an Italian grave, and the texts that would decide the question were written four hundred years after both men were dead.
suggested_refs: The Acts of Saint Elmo, the vehicle of the Antioch conflation
sources: Catholic Encyclopedia (1913), cited at one remove via en.wikipedia

stops.name: Nicomedia, the edict published
stops.date_confidence: attested. en.wikipedia 'Diocletianic Persecution' dates the razing of the Nicomedia church to 23 February 303, the feast of the Terminalia, and the publication of the Edict against the Christians to the following day. Pin inherited byte-identical from saint_acacius.journey.json and saint_blaise.journey.json. The link to Erasmus is thematic and not documentary: no record places him at Nicomedia.
stops.campa: On the feast of the Terminalia, Diocletian orders the new church at Nicomedia razed, and the Edict against the Christians is published the next day. Scripture is to be burned, churches levelled, Christians in office stripped of rank. The order goes out from the eastern capital along every road the empire has, and the persecution it opens will carry off Blaise at Sebastea, Cyriacus on the Via Salaria, Pantaleon in this city, and Acacius at Byzantium, all of them named later beside Erasmus among the Fourteen.
suggested_refs: The imperial palace quarter at Nicomedia, modern Izmit, where the edict was posted

stops.name: Mount Lebanon, seven years and a raven
stops.date_confidence: legend, and the place is contested. it.wikipedia says only that he took refuge seven years in a cave, unnamed and unlocated; the Anglophone summary names Mount Lebanon and adds the raven. No source names a peak, a valley or a spring. The pin is set in the Qadisha and Cedars of God tract, the range's famous hermitage country, explicitly as an illustration and not as an attested site.
stops.campa: With the persecution closing on his diocese, Erasmus goes up into the cedar country of Mount Lebanon and lives seven years in a cave. A raven brings him food. The Italian tradition keeps the seven years and the cave and refuses to name the mountain; the English keeps the mountain and adds the bird. No text names a peak, a valley or a spring. The pin here is set in the Qadisha, the gorge of the hermits, which is where such a man would be put by anyone telling the story afterwards, and is offered as exactly that.
suggested_refs: The Qadisha valley and the Cedars of God, the hermitage country of Mount Lebanon

stops.name: Mount Lebanon, the angel sends him down
stops.date_confidence: legend. en.wikipedia reports the angelic vision as part of the traditional Acts; no independent attestation exists, and the placeholder coordinate is the same illustrative Qadisha pin as the preceding stop.
stops.campa: An angel stands in the mouth of the cave and tells him the hiding is over: go back to the city and preach. Seven years of silence end in one sentence. He goes. It is the hinge the legend needs, because a hermit fed by ravens does not get arrested and a bishop preaching in a city does, and the Passio has a martyrdom to deliver. He comes down out of the cedars in the year the edict is posted at Nicomedia, walking toward a court that will spend the rest of the text inventing ways to kill him.
suggested_refs: The angelic vision episode in the traditional Acts of Saint Elmo

stops.name: Antioch, the soldiers find him
stops.date_confidence: legend, with a historical strain flagged. Diocletian's court sits ordinarily at Nicomedia and used Antioch only intermittently, chiefly during the Persian campaigns of the mid-290s. No administrative record puts the emperor in Syria in 303.
stops.campa: Soldiers take him and bring him before Diocletian at Antioch. Historically the emperor's court sits at Nicomedia and comes to Antioch only in passing, chiefly during the Persian campaigns of the 290s, and no administrative record puts him in Syria in this year. The legend does not care. It needs an emperor and a bishop in one room and it puts them there. What follows in the Golden Legend is not a trial. It is a catalogue of instruments, each tried in turn, each failing, the bishop answering after every failure.
suggested_refs: The itinerary of Diocletian for 303, which does not include Antioch
sources: catholic.org, saint profile of Saint Erasmus

stops.name: Antioch, the refusal before the emperor
stops.date_confidence: legend as event, attested as text. The quotation is verbatim from Caxton's Golden Legend as printed by Wynkyn de Worde in 1527; what it attests is what the sixteenth century was reading, not what was said in Syria.
stops.campa: The emperor orders him to sacrifice to the gods of Rome. Erasmus answers standing. He will not forsake the God who made heaven and hell and everything in them, not for anything that can be done to his body, because that God took flesh and tasted a bitter death for him and for all sinners. The answer is the whole plot given away in advance: nothing the empire can do to a man matters, and the empire will now spend the rest of the text proving that it cannot make him say otherwise.
stops.quote: Almighty God, that made all things, hath wrought heaven and hell and all that is therein, him will I not forsake for no thing that can or may be done to me, for his goodly grace hath given to me such grace, and to other his chosen friends, that he was made man and hath tasted and suffered the bitter death for me and for all sinners.
stops.quote_source: The Golden Legend, Caxton's translation as printed by Wynken de Worde, 1527, 'Life of Saint Erasmus'; text at catholicsaints.info
suggested_refs: Wynken de Worde's 1527 English Golden Legend, 'Life of Saint Erasmus'
sources: The Golden Legend (Caxton, de Worde 1527) via catholicsaints.info

stops.name: Antioch, the leaden mallets
stops.date_confidence: legend as event, attested as text. The Caxton wording is the narrator's, describing the first torment ordered.
stops.campa: The first instrument is the simplest. He is beaten with mallets of lead until, in the printer's phrase, every vein in him must break and burst. He does not die. The text moves straight to the next device without pausing over the failure, and this is the rhythm of the whole passion: an ingenuity of the state, applied in full, producing nothing. Formia will remember a bishop. Germany, five centuries from now, will remember only the last of these machines, and will put it in his hands to hold.
stops.quote: beaten so cruelly with leaden malles, that all his veins must break and burst
stops.quote_source: The Golden Legend, Caxton's translation as printed by Wynken de Worde, 1527, 'Life of Saint Erasmus'; via catholicsaints.info
suggested_refs: The catalogue of torments in the Life of Saint Erasmus, Golden Legend
sources: The Golden Legend (Caxton, de Worde 1527) via catholicsaints.info

stops.name: Antioch, the burning coat
stops.date_confidence: legend as event, attested as text. The speech is placed by the source immediately before he is clad in the heated metal coat.
stops.campa: A coat of metal is heated until it glows and put on his naked body. Before they dress him in it he says that his Lord has done and suffered more for him than he has deserved, and that he will therefore suffer everything he is able to suffer, and commits himself wholly to grace. He is also put into a pit of snakes, adders and paddocks, and into a pan seething with rosin, pitch, brimstone, lead and oil, which is poured into his mouth. He comes out of each of them alive.
stops.quote: My Lord and my God hath for me so much done and suffered more than I have deserved. Wherefore I will suffer all that I may suffer for him, for he hath deserved it so highly against me and against all sinners, therefore I tell you for certain that I will never forsake him, suffer all that I may suffer for his holy name, and I commit me wholly to his holy grace.
stops.quote_source: The Golden Legend, Caxton's translation as printed by Wynken de Worde, 1527, 'Life of Saint Erasmus'; via catholicsaints.info
suggested_refs: The burning coat, the pit of adders and the seething pan, three consecutive torments in the Caxton text
sources: The Golden Legend (Caxton, de Worde 1527) via catholicsaints.info

stops.name: Antioch, the teeth drawn with pincers
stops.date_confidence: legend as event, attested as text. The iron cards of the same passage are wool-combers' carding rakes, the fixed emblem of Blaise of Sebastea and used on him in a parallel Passio of the same generation.
stops.campa: His teeth are drawn out of his head with iron pincers and his skin is carded with iron cards, the combs used on wool. Nothing is left of his mouth and nothing changes in what comes out of it. The same combs are being used on Blaise at Sebastea in the same generation of legends, and Blaise will be given them as his emblem while Erasmus is given the windlass. The instruments of these passions circulate between the saints like tools in a shared workshop, and the one that sticks is whichever a town carved first.
stops.quote: commanded his teeth to be plucked out of his head with iron pincers
stops.quote_source: The Golden Legend, Caxton's translation as printed by Wynken de Worde, 1527, 'Life of Saint Erasmus'; via catholicsaints.info
suggested_refs: The iron carding-combs, shared instrument of the passions of Erasmus and of Blaise of Sebastea
sources: The Golden Legend (Caxton, de Worde 1527) via catholicsaints.info

stops.name: Antioch, the bed of roses on the fire
stops.date_confidence: legend as event, attested as text. The source places the speech during the roasting.
stops.campa: They lay him on a fire to roast him and he speaks from inside it, telling them he lies better than he is worthy, on a bed strewn with sweet roses, and that he can see the everlasting light and the Son of God seated at the right hand of the Father. The remark is the centre of the English text. The torment is not endured; it is not there at all. Later ages will call this legendary and mean the word as a dismissal, but the compilers knew what they were writing and were not trying to report a fire.
stops.quote: I lie here better than I am worthy, for I lie upon a bed well strewed with sweet roses, and I see the light everlasting, the Son of God, sitting on the right hand of his Father.
stops.quote_source: The Golden Legend, Caxton's translation as printed by Wynken de Worde, 1527, 'Life of Saint Erasmus'; via catholicsaints.info
suggested_refs: The roasting episode in the Caxton Life of Saint Erasmus
sources: The Golden Legend (Caxton, de Worde 1527) via catholicsaints.info

stops.name: Antioch, the angel opens the prison
stops.date_confidence: legend. en.wikipedia and CatholicSaints.info both carry the angelic release; no independent attestation.
stops.campa: He is put back in the cell and an angel opens it. Coming out, he asks God where he has been and blesses the name in the same breath, the only complaint anywhere in the text and it lasts four words. The door stands open on a road he has not been told to take. The escape is what moves the story west out of Syria: an imprisoned bishop dies in Antioch and the file closes, a freed one walks to Lycia and picks up a second act. From here the Passio stops being about an emperor and becomes about a crowd.
stops.quote: O God, where hast thou been? blessed be thy name.
stops.quote_source: The Golden Legend, Caxton's translation as printed by Wynken de Worde, 1527, 'Life of Saint Erasmus'; via catholicsaints.info
suggested_refs: The angelic release from the Antioch prison in the Acts of Saint Elmo

stops.name: Myra, the dead son raised
stops.date_confidence: legend, on a placeholder coordinate. en.wikipedia names only the province, Lycia, and no town. Myra is pinned as the province's best-known city and nothing more; it becomes the Lycian capital only in 325, twenty-two years after these events. The research pool's 36.2508, 29.9744 is neither Myra (36.2592, 29.9853) nor Demre town centre (36.2440, 29.9853); corrected here.
stops.campa: In Lycia, the mountainous Roman province on the southern coast of Asia Minor, a citizen's son is dead and Erasmus raises him. The witnesses go to baptism in a mass. No source names the town; the pin is set at Myra, which is the province's best-known city and will not become its capital for another twenty-two years, and it is offered as an illustration and not as a location. This same coast will keep another bishop who raises the dead and guards sailors, and at sea the two patronages will get confused.
suggested_refs: The Lycian coast and the site of Myra at modern Demre, Turkey

stops.name: Lycia, the word reaches Maximian
stops.date_confidence: legend, on the same Myra placeholder. The involvement of Maximian is one of the internal strains the historians cite: the western Augustus has no jurisdiction in Lycia, and the two tetrarchic courts are not documented passing provincial preachers between them.
stops.campa: The conversions are too many to go unreported. Word reaches Maximian Herculius, Diocletian's colleague in the West and the harder of the two men on this subject, and he orders the bishop taken again. The legend has now used both emperors, which is one of the reasons the historians distrust it: the western Augustus holds no jurisdiction in Lycia, and the two courts are not in the habit of passing provincial preachers to each other. The Passio wants the full weight of the empire and simply takes it.
suggested_refs: The division of the tetrarchy, under which Lycia falls to the eastern and not the western Augustus

stops.name: A hillside in Lycia, the barrel of spikes
stops.date_confidence: legend, on the same Myra placeholder. No hillside and no town are named in any source. No Roman legal or narrative source reachable here attests a spiked barrel as a penalty; that absence is recorded as a gap rather than argued.
stops.campa: He is shut in a barrel driven full of spikes and rolled down a hill. He survives it. No hillside is named and no town, so the pin holds at the Myra placeholder because the text gives nothing else to hold to. This episode shows what kind of document the Passio is: a barrel studded with nails is not a Roman penalty attested anywhere reachable in Roman law. It is a thing imagined by a later century for a saint who has already survived fire and lead and needs something new done to him.
stops.quote: O Almighty God, have mercy upon me.
stops.quote_source: The Golden Legend, Caxton's translation as printed by Wynken de Worde, 1527, 'Life of Saint Erasmus'; via catholicsaints.info
suggested_refs: The spiked barrel episode, without precedent in attested Roman penal practice
sources: The Golden Legend (Caxton, de Worde 1527) via catholicsaints.info

stops.name: Salona in Illyricum, the windlass
stops.date_confidence: legend, on a placeholder coordinate, and one half of an unresolved contradiction. en.wikipedia names only the province. Salona, capital of Roman Dalmatia and the ground of many other martyrdoms, is pinned as a stand-in. The rival account, at Formia, is pinned separately on the same date; neither source yields and neither is preferred here.
stops.campa: The English tradition carries him across the Adriatic to Illyricum and kills him there: his belly opened, his intestines wound out on a windlass. No town is named. Salona, the capital of Roman Dalmatia and the ground of a dozen other martyrdoms, holds the pin as a stand-in. This is the death that made the image. The image made the patronage, and the patronage put his name on the fire that plays at a masthead in a storm. Poussin will paint the windlass over an altar in St Peter's thirteen centuries later.
stops.quote: cut him upon his belly, and wound out his guts or bowels out of his blessed body
stops.quote_source: The Golden Legend, Caxton's translation as printed by Wynken de Worde, 1527, 'Life of Saint Erasmus'; via catholicsaints.info
suggested_refs: The ruins of Salona near Split, Croatia, pinned as an illustrative stand-in for an unnamed Illyrian site
sources: The Golden Legend (Caxton, de Worde 1527) via catholicsaints.info

stops.name: Formia, the archangel brings him home
stops.date_confidence: legend, and the other half of the contradiction. it.wikipedia and the local Gaeta and Formia cult have the archangel Michael bring him to Formia, where he dies seven days later, with no disembowelment mentioned at all. The two accounts cannot both be literally true; both are carried, six hundred miles apart on one date, flagged rather than reconciled.
stops.campa: The Italian tradition tells it otherwise. The archangel Michael takes him out of the East and sets him down at Formia, his own see on the Tyrrhenian coast, and there is no windlass in the account at all. The two versions cannot both be true and neither source yields to the other. The Italian article goes further and proposes that the windlass was never a weapon: that it is a ship's winch out of the paintings, the emblem of a patronage he acquired later, misread by people who wanted an instrument.
stops.quote: O Almighty God, Father of heaven, thy will be fulfilled in me.
stops.quote_source: The Golden Legend, Caxton's translation as printed by Wynken de Worde, 1527, 'Life of Saint Erasmus'; via catholicsaints.info
suggested_refs: The argano hypothesis advanced by it.wikipedia, that the windlass is a misread ship's winch
sources: The Golden Legend (Caxton, de Worde 1527) via catholicsaints.info

stops.name: Formia, the seventh day
stops.date_confidence: legend for the death, attested for the feast. 2 June is the day the church keeps and is attested in the Hieronymian Martyrology by roughly 600; whether it marks a death, a burial, or a free slot in a later calendar, nothing consulted can say.
stops.campa: Seven days after Michael sets him down he dies, on a Sunday by the reckoning of the English text, commending his spirit. The feast the church keeps is the second of June. Whether that is the day of a death at Formia, or of a burial, or a day some later calendar happened to have free, nothing consulted can say. The town takes the body and keeps it, and for the next five hundred years the only verifiable fact in this whole life is that a church in Formia has a grave in it that people visit.
stops.quote: O Lord in thy hands yield I my spirit, and this Sunday receive my soul into thy peace and rest.
stops.quote_source: The Golden Legend, Caxton's translation as printed by Wynken de Worde, 1527, 'Life of Saint Erasmus'; via catholicsaints.info
suggested_refs: The feast of 2 June, attested in the Hieronymian Martyrology
sources: The Golden Legend (Caxton, de Worde 1527) via catholicsaints.info

segments.name: Formia and Gaeta: the Relics Move Twice

stops.name: Formia, the Passio written and misattributed
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the century. it.wikipedia: 'La Passio che narra la vita di sant'Erasmo risale al VI secolo.' Author unknown, place of composition unknown. 550 is a mid-century placeholder. The research pool misdescribed the Gelasius problem; the fault is a misattribution to the wrong Gelasius, corrected here.
stops.campa: The Passio that carries everything above is written in the sixth century, author unknown. A later age attributes it to a Pope Gelasius and picks the wrong one: Gelasius II, who reigned for a single year in 1118, six centuries after the text. Gelasius I, who reigned from 492 to 496, sits adjacent to the century in question and would at least have been possible. This is what happens to a document nobody holds an independent copy of, and it is why the Catholic Encyclopedia says the passio has no historical basis.
suggested_refs: The sixth-century Passio of Erasmus, misattributed in the Middle Ages to Pope Gelasius II
sources: Catholic Encyclopedia (1913), cited at one remove via en.wikipedia

stops.name: Formia, Gregory names the church that holds him
stops.date_confidence: attested, and the earliest hard anchor in the dossier. Pope Gregory the Great (590 to 604) reports the body kept at a church in Formia. The pool called the building 'Formia Cathedral'; the see of Formiae was extinguished and its rights carried to Gaeta, so no such building survives. The coordinate is an approximate centroid of the Castellone district; no excavated plan was located.
stops.campa: Pope Gregory the Great writes that the body of Erasmus is kept and venerated at a church in Formia. This is the earliest hard anchor in the file: not a life, not a martyrdom, a location. The see is later extinguished and its rights carried to Gaeta, so no cathedral of Formia survives to be excavated. What stands on the ground now is the three-naved church of Sant'Erasmo Vescovo e Martire in the Castellone quarter, Renaissance in its fabric, sitting on or near the tradition.
suggested_refs: The church of Sant'Erasmo Vescovo e Martire in the Castellone quarter of Formia
sources: catholic.org, saint profile citing Gregory the Great

stops.name: Rome, the feast enters the Martyrology
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the fact, approximate as to the date. it.wikipedia reports the 2 June feast in the Hieronymian Martyrology, one of the oldest surviving Western martyrologies. 600 is a placeholder for the martyrology's working period. Rome pin inherited byte-identical from catorce_santos_ayudantes.journey.json.
stops.campa: The second of June enters the Hieronymian Martyrology, one of the oldest surviving lists of the Western dead. This is the moment Erasmus becomes an entry rather than a story: a name, a day, a place of burial, filed alongside hundreds of others whose passiones nobody will ever be able to check either. The list outlasts the text. Long after the Catholic Encyclopedia calls the life baseless, the date will still be there, because a calendar does not have to believe anything to keep working.
suggested_refs: The Martyrologium Hieronymianum, carrying Erasmus at 2 June

stops.name: Formia, the Saracens burn the town
stops.date_confidence: attested. Both the English and Italian articles date the destruction of old Formiae by Saracen raiders to 842; the transfer of the cult is dated only as after it.
stops.campa: Saracen raiders come ashore and destroy old Formiae. The town does not recover as a see, and what is portable leaves. Six years earlier the abbey of Corvey on the Weser had received the bones of Vitus from Saint-Denis, the first of the fourteen planted in German ground by deliberate policy. Erasmus moves in the same ninth-century wave of translation and in the opposite spirit: not policy, flight. The relics go up the coast in the hands of the people carrying them.
suggested_refs: The ruins of old Formiae, destroyed by Saracen raiders in 842

stops.name: Gaeta, carried from the burning see
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year, undated within it. Pin inherited byte-identical from catorce_santos_ayudantes.journey.json, which already narrates this transfer from the company's side. en.wikipedia 'Gaeta Cathedral' names the church and the bishop, both of which the research pool omitted.
stops.campa: Bishop John III brings the relics into Gaeta and puts them in the church of Santa Maria del Parco, which is already standing. There they are hidden. The atlas holds this stop already from the other side: the file of the Fourteen Holy Helpers records the same year, the same raid, the same carrying up the coast, and notes that from here Erasmus travels under a second name and takes the sailors with him. This file arrives at the same pin from the direction of the man instead of the company.
suggested_refs: The church of Santa Maria del Parco at Gaeta, first hiding place of the relics

stops.name: Gaeta, Bishop Bono finds them again
stops.date_confidence: attested by it.wikipedia, which also settles the order: 'furono ritrovate nel 917 dal vescovo Bono. Sant'Erasmo fu quindi proclamato patrono della citta.' The research pool dated the patronage to 850, before the rediscovery; corrected.
stops.campa: Seventy-five years in hiding, and Bishop Bono of Gaeta rediscovers the relics. The city proclaims Erasmus its patron. The patronage begins here and not in the ninth century, whatever the handbooks say: the Italian source puts the proclamation plainly after the inventio. A hidden body is a body nobody can steal. A found body is a civic asset, and Gaeta from this point on is a town with a saint in it, and builds accordingly, and says so on the front of the building.
suggested_refs: The 917 inventio of the relics of Erasmus by Bishop Bono of Gaeta

stops.name: Gaeta, Paschal II consecrates the cathedral
stops.date_confidence: attested. en.wikipedia 'Gaeta Cathedral' gives 22 January 1106 and coordinates 41.208944, 13.586806. The research pool carried 1108 at 41.2072, 13.5711, about 1.3 km west of the building, and called the year vague across sources while its own chronology lens said 1106; both errors corrected.
stops.campa: On the twenty-second of January Pope Paschal II consecrates the new cathedral of Gaeta, dedicated to Saints Erasmus and Marcian together with Saint Mary of the Assumption. The relics move into it. A bishop of a town that no longer exists now has a cathedral in a town that does, eight hundred years after his death and two and a half centuries after the raid that moved him. Every second of June the reliquaries go through the streets, in a rite whose first year no source consulted will name.
suggested_refs: The Basilica Cattedrale dei Santi Erasmo e Marciano e Santa Maria Assunta, Gaeta

segments.name: Elmo: the Name Shortens and Goes to Sea

stops.name: Naples, the church on the Vomero
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the tenth-century church and the contraction, approximate as to the year. en.wikipedia 'Castel Sant'Elmo' dates the church to the tenth century without a year; 950 is a placeholder.
stops.campa: On the hill above Naples that will be called the Vomero there stands a tenth-century church dedicated to Sant'Erasmo. Neapolitan mouths shorten it: Erasmo to Ermo to Elmo. The saint acquires the name he will carry at sea in every European language. No text orders the change and no decree ratifies it. It comes off the ordinary wear of people saying a word too often, and nobody decides any part of it. The hill keeps the shortened form permanently, and so does the fire.
suggested_refs: The tenth-century church of Sant'Erasmo on the Vomero, origin of the Neapolitan toponym Sant'Elmo

stops.name: The central Mediterranean, the fire takes his name
stops.date_confidence: attested as a naming tradition, undatable as an event. The coordinate is a nominal central-Mediterranean point: the phenomenon has no location, and the naming was never universal even within Christian seafaring.
stops.campa: Sailors see a blue-white brush of light stand up on the mastheads and yardarms in a storm and call it St Elmo's fire, taking it for a sign that the danger is going off. The naming is never universal. Welsh crews call the same light the candles of the Holy Ghost, or the candles of St David; Russian crews give it to St Nicholas, or call it St Peter's lights; elsewhere it is St Helen's fire, or St Hermes' fire. The coordinate here is nominal. The phenomenon has no location at all.
suggested_refs: The corposant, corona discharge at mastheads, named for Erasmus across Latin Christian seafaring

stops.name: Naples, castrum Sancti Erasmi
stops.date_confidence: attested. Coordinate matches en.wikipedia 'Castel Sant'Elmo' exactly. The research pool credited Charles of Anjou with converting the site into a fortress; en.wiki documents only a structure there from 1275 under Charles I, with the fortress commissioned by Robert of Anjou from 1329 and built by Tino da Camaino until his death in 1343, called a castrum by 1336. The 1348 attestation of the name is correct.
stops.campa: There is a structure on the site from 1275 under Charles I of Anjou, a walled fortified residence. Robert of Anjou commissions the fortress from 1329, and Tino da Camaino builds it until he dies in 1343; it is called a castrum by 1336, and in 1348 the documents give the name in full: castrum Sancti Erasmi. Angevin, then Aragonese, then Spanish, the castle holds the Naples skyline to this day under the contracted name of a bishop nobody there can any longer place.
suggested_refs: Castel Sant'Elmo on the Vomero, attested as castrum Sancti Erasmi in 1348

stops.name: Puerto San Julian, the lights on the mastheads
stops.date_confidence: placeholder, heavily hedged. en.wikipedia gives only 'Antonio Pigafetta's journal of his 1519 to 1522 voyage with Ferdinand Magellan', with no year within the voyage and no position. The research pool pinned -52.6, -68.5, the Atlantic mouth of the Strait of Magellan, in April 1520, which is internally impossible: the fleet did not enter the strait until 21 October 1520. Moved here to the Patagonian wintering anchorage.
stops.campa: Antonio Pigafetta, keeping the journal of Magellan's circumnavigation, records glowing lights standing on the ships' mastheads in a storm, and the crews taking them for a favourable sign. The Portuguese call that light corpo santo. Pigafetta gives no date and no position; the voyage runs from 1519 to 1522, and the fleet winters at Puerto San Julian on the Patagonian coast. The pin sits there for want of anything better, and is entered as a guess about a sighting that has no place attached to it.
suggested_refs: Antonio Pigafetta's journal of the Magellan circumnavigation, 1519 to 1522

stops.name: Valletta, the fort called Sant'Ermu
stops.date_confidence: attested for the construction date and the dedication.
stops.campa: The Knights of St John raise a fort on the point at the mouth of the Grand Harbour and name it for Sant'Ermu. Thirteen years later, in 1565, the Ottomans will spend a month and thousands of men taking it, and its defenders will die to the last man. The saint on the gate is the bishop of Formia, arrived here by way of a shortened Neapolitan word and a light on a masthead, with no connection to Malta, the sea, or soldiering in any text about his life.
suggested_refs: Fort St Elmo, Valletta, built 1552 and besieged in 1565

stops.name: Lisbon, the fire enters the epic
stops.date_confidence: attested as literary attestation, and a correction of 75 years. en.wikipedia says the phenomenon 'is also described in The Lusiads (1572), the epic account of the voyages of discovery of Vasco da Gama'. The research pool logged this as a sighting recorded on da Gama's 1497 voyage; it is Camoes's poem, published in 1572, and nothing of the kind.
stops.campa: Luis de Camoes publishes Os Lusiadas, the epic of the Portuguese discoveries and of Vasco da Gama's road to India, and puts the living light on the rigging into it. This is a poem of 1572, not a ship's log of 1497. What it attests is not a sighting but a convention: by the later sixteenth century the fire is literary furniture, a thing any reader of a sea narrative is expected to recognise on sight, and the saint's name on it needs no gloss for anybody.
suggested_refs: Luis de Camoes, Os Lusiadas (1572), describing the corposant on the rigging

stops.name: The Rio de la Plata, the Beagle
stops.date_confidence: attested as an observation, placeholder as a position. en.wikipedia records Darwin observing St Elmo's fire aboard HMS Beagle and gives no location; the pin is set in the Rio de la Plata, where the Beagle worked in these years, and is a guess.
stops.campa: Charles Darwin, aboard HMS Beagle, records the phenomenon. Three hundred years of Atlantic sailing separate him from Pigafetta and the name has not changed. It will survive the explanation too: corona discharge from a grounded conductor standing in a strong electric field, which is what a masthead is. The pin is set in the Rio de la Plata, where the Beagle worked in these years, and the source gives no position at all. Erasmus by now has no cult attached to the light. He has only the name on it.
suggested_refs: Darwin's record of St Elmo's fire aboard HMS Beagle

stops.name: Regensburg, the fresco gathers them
stops.date_confidence: attested for the Regensburg fresco and glass, dated 1320 to 1360 in catorce_santos_ayudantes.journey.json, from which this pin is inherited byte-identical. 1350 is the mid-point.
stops.campa: In the Dominican church at Regensburg the fourteen are painted together, and in the cathedral glass shortly after. The plague is working through the empire, and a devotion assembles that offers one prayer to a whole company instead of fourteen prayers to fourteen saints. Erasmus is in it from the start. So are Blaise of Sebastea, Cyriacus the Roman deacon, Acacius the Cappadocian centurion, Denis of Paris, Barbara, Catherine of Alexandria and Christopher. Most of them died in the persecution he did.
suggested_refs: The Fourteen Holy Helpers fresco in the Dominican church at Regensburg

stops.name: Nuremberg, the order closes at fourteen
stops.date_confidence: attested. Pin and date inherited byte-identical from catorce_santos_ayudantes.journey.json, which records the company fixed by about 1400 and kept jointly at Regensburg, Bamberg, Wurzburg and Nuremberg.
stops.campa: By about 1400 the list is fixed and held in common at Regensburg, Bamberg, Wurzburg and Nuremberg: Acacius, Barbara, Blaise, Catherine, Christopher, Cyriacus, Denis, Erasmus, Eustace, George, Giles, Margaret, Pantaleon, Vitus. Fourteen and no more. Erasmus, an Italian bishop of a town destroyed five hundred years earlier, is now a fixed member of a German devotional company, invoked in a language he never heard, against an ailment his own legend never says he cured.
suggested_refs: The closed roster of the Vierzehn Nothelfer, fixed by about 1400

stops.name: Franconia, the belly and the beasts
stops.date_confidence: attested for the patronage, inferred for its cause. en.wikipedia lists colic, abdominal pain, intestinal ailments, labour pains and cattle pests. The sources themselves read the patronage as arising from the disembowelment legend; there is no healing episode anywhere in the life to support it. Pin shared with the Nuremberg stop for want of a single site.
stops.campa: Inland, where nobody works a winch, the same picture is read a second way, and Erasmus becomes the saint of the belly: colic, cramp, intestinal disease, the pains of labour. Villages add the health of cattle, and a 1908 devotional source quoted in the atlas names him with George, Pantaleon and Vitus for animals struck by plague. Blaise takes the throat from a fishbone he removes in the text. Erasmus takes the gut from a wound he receives, which is a different logic entirely.
suggested_refs: The Nothelfer patronage scheme, assigning Erasmus the abdomen

stops.name: Vierzehnheiligen, the shepherd sees the fourteen children
stops.date_confidence: attested as tradition, dated 1445 to 1446 by en.wikipedia and by catorce_santos_ayudantes.journey.json, from which this pin and date are inherited byte-identical. The first altar is consecrated in 1448.
stops.campa: A shepherd of the abbey of Langheim, Hermann Leicht, sees a child in the field, and then fourteen children, who tell him they are the fourteen helpers and want a chapel on the spot. An altar is consecrated two years later. The place takes the name Vierzehnheiligen, fourteen saints. Erasmus is one of the children standing in that field. A Baroque basilica will rise here between 1743 and 1772, and it is the architectural home of his cult far more than Gaeta ever was, counted in visitors.
suggested_refs: The Basilica of the Fourteen Holy Helpers at Vierzehnheiligen, built 1743 to 1772

stops.name: Rome, Nicholas V attaches indulgences
stops.date_confidence: attested. Pin and date inherited byte-identical from catorce_santos_ayudantes.journey.json.
stops.campa: Pope Nicholas V attaches indulgences to devotion of the Fourteen Holy Helpers, and the company acquires an institutional standing to match the popular one. This is the high water of Erasmus in the north. For a century he is one of the fourteen names a German villager can be relied on to know, painted on altarpieces from the Danube to the Weser, holding the winch that Gaeta's sailors read as their own gear and that Franconia reads as the thing that killed him.
suggested_refs: The indulgences of Nicholas V for the devotion of the Fourteen Holy Helpers, 1450

segments.name: The Windlass, the Skull, the Calendar

stops.name: London, the legend goes into English print
stops.date_confidence: attested. Wynken de Worde's 1527 English edition of the Golden Legend is the printing from which every verbatim quotation in this file is taken. The coordinate is nominal for the City of London.
stops.campa: Wynken de Worde prints an English Golden Legend, and the Life of Saint Erasmus goes into vernacular circulation: the mallets, the adders, the burning coat, the pincers, the bed of roses, the guts wound out. Every quotation carried in this file comes from that printing. It is not a record of anything that happened in 303. It is what the sixteenth century was reading, in English, about a man of whose life the one documented fact is that Gregory the Great knew where the body was.
suggested_refs: Wynken de Worde's 1527 English edition of the Golden Legend
sources: The Golden Legend (Caxton, de Worde 1527) via catholicsaints.info

stops.name: Vatican, Poussin over the altar
stops.date_confidence: attested. Poussin's Martyrdom of Saint Erasmus was painted 1628 to 1629 for an altar in the north transept of St Peter's; a mosaic copy now hangs there and the canvas is in the Vatican Pinacoteca.
stops.campa: Nicolas Poussin paints the Martyrdom of Saint Erasmus for an altar in the north transept of St Peter's: the bishop on his back, the windlass turning, the executioner's hands in the opened belly, an angel overhead with the palm. A mosaic copy hangs there now and the canvas is in the Pinacoteca. The picture is the most public thing about him, and it depicts the episode the Catholic Encyclopedia will call baseless. Rome keeps the image and disbelieves the event and finds no difficulty in that.
suggested_refs: Nicolas Poussin, The Martyrdom of Saint Erasmus, 1628 to 1629, Vatican Pinacoteca

stops.name: Munich, the skull purported
stops.date_confidence: hedged in the source and hedged here; no date exists. en.wikipedia says the skull 'is purported to be in St. Peter's Church, Munich', and the Peterskirche article says only that relics of Munditia and of Erasmus of Formia are venerated there, without calling any of them a skull. The research pool tagged this attested; downgraded to reconstruction. 1700 is a bare placeholder to keep the stop in sequence.
stops.campa: The skull of Erasmus is said to be at St Peter's church in Munich, the Peterskirche. The wording matters. The English article says purported, and the church's own article says only that relics of Erasmus and of Munditia are venerated there, without calling any of them a skull. Further body parts attributed to him are reported dispersed across Europe, and no source consulted names the churches. No original grave of Erasmus has ever been opened or excavated anywhere, at Formia or elsewhere.
suggested_refs: The Peterskirche, Munich, where relics of Erasmus and of Munditia are venerated

stops.name: Bassiano, the towns that keep him
stops.date_confidence: attested for the patronages, undated as a stop. The research pool put Bassiano at 41.5017, 13.1108, roughly 8 km wrong; corrected to approximately 41.550, 13.033. The pool also omitted Roccagorga from en.wikipedia's patronage list. Santeramo in Colle sits at approximately 40.800, 16.767. 1900 is a nominal date for a continuing modern cult.
stops.campa: Bassiano in the Lepini hills of Lazio keeps Erasmus as its patron, and so do Roccagorga nearby, Santeramo in Colle down in Puglia, Formia, and Gaeta. The Puglian town carries his name inside its own: Santeramo, Sant'Erasmo. These are living cults, with processions and bands and a fixed day in June, and not one of them requires the Passio to be true. What a patronal town keeps is a name, a date, and the right to be the place that has him. None of the five has a grave, and none of them has ever needed one.
suggested_refs: The patronal towns of Erasmus: Gaeta, Formia, Bassiano, Roccagorga, Santeramo in Colle

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the barrio on the third hill
stops.date_confidence: nominal, and entered as such. Pin and date inherited byte-identical from catorce_santos_ayudantes.journey.json, which shares the San Cristobal pin with emin_arslan.journey.json. No relic, legend or local story of Erasmus attaches to it; the stop records the reach of the company, not of the man.
stops.campa: The barrio of San Cristobal carries a pin the atlas already shares between the Fourteen Holy Helpers and Emin Arslan, the Ottoman consul who worked these streets. Erasmus reaches Buenos Aires the way the whole company reaches it, in a street grid and a set of parish names carried by an immigrant city, with no relic and no local story of his own. The pin is nominal and is entered as such. A saint can travel sixteen centuries and eleven thousand kilometres and arrive as a word on a corner.
suggested_refs: The barrio of San Cristobal, Buenos Aires, shared nominal pin of the Fourteen Holy Helpers

stops.name: Rome, four names come off the calendar
stops.date_confidence: attested. Pin and date inherited byte-identical from catorce_santos_ayudantes.journey.json. No document consulted explains why Erasmus was spared a revision that removed four of his own company on grounds of unverifiable historicity.
stops.campa: The revision of the General Roman Calendar drops the universal feasts of Barbara, Catherine of Alexandria, Christopher and Margaret of Antioch on grounds of unverifiable historicity. Erasmus, whose entire passion the Catholic Encyclopedia had called baseless in 1913, is left alone. His feast stays at the second of June in the Roman Martyrology. Four of his fourteen companions come off and he does not, and no document consulted explains the distinction. Gaeta and Formia keep the day either way.
suggested_refs: The 1969 revision of the General Roman Calendar and the surviving 2 June entry in the Roman Martyrology
